q: A malt bottled at 43 percent turns cloudy the moment a guest adds a splash of water. Which treatment would have prevented that haze, and is often left out on purpose?
exp: Long-chain fatty esters drop out of solution when a spirit is chilled or watered below about 46 percent, which is a cosmetic problem and nothing more. Filtering them out at low temperature removes the haze and, many argue, some texture with it, so bottlings at 46 percent and above frequently skip it.

q: A label reads blended malt Scotch whisky and names no distillery anywhere on it. What is in the bottle?
opts: Malt whiskies from more than one distillery, and no grain
Malt whisky from one distillery, married from several casks
Malt and grain whisky drawn from one distillery
Grain whiskies from several distilleries with a little malt added
exp: Not a drop of grain whisky may go in, and the malt has to come from two distilleries or more. The category was called vatted malt until the Scotch Whisky Regulations settled the naming in 2009. Blended Scotch is the different animal: malt whisky married with grain whisky from a column still, which is what the great majority of Scotch sold in the world is.

q: Five whisky localities and regions are protected under the Scotch Whisky Regulations, and one of them is a single island rather than a stretch of the mainland. Which?
exp: The regulations protect five: Highland, Lowland, Speyside, Campbeltown and Islay. Orkney, Skye, Jura, Mull and Arran all distil, but they sit inside the Highland region rather than standing on their own.

q: Thirty distilleries once crowded a single harbour town on the Kintyre peninsula, and its name survives as one of Scotland's protected whisky regions. Name the town.
exp: The town collapsed as a whisky centre in the 1920s and ran for decades on a couple of working distilleries, but the region was never struck off. What survived there also kept practices that vanished elsewhere, floor malting among them.

q: Dufftown, Rothes and Craigellachie all sit inside the same protected Scotch whisky region, clustered around one river valley. Name the region.
exp: The Spey and its tributaries drain the whole zone, and those towns are its distilling centres. A Speyside whisky may also be labelled Highland, since the zone sits geographically inside the Highland region, but the reverse is not permitted.

q: Peating is quoted in parts per million measured on the malt, and the figure counts one family of compounds picked up from the kiln smoke. Name that family.
exp: A good deal of the phenol is lost through fermentation and distillation, so the number on a bag of malt overstates what reaches the glass by a wide margin. Guaiacol and the cresols sit within that family and carry the tar, smoke and iodine notes.

q: Oak is not the only cask requirement in the Scotch rules, which also set a limit on the size of the vessel. What is that maximum?
exp: Anything larger falls outside the definition, which rules out the great vats used elsewhere for solera-style ageing. Inside the limit the range is wide, from the 200 litre ex-bourbon barrel through the 250 litre hogshead to the 500 litre sherry butt.

q: Colour is the one adjustment a Scotch producer may still make in the vat, and a single additive is permitted for it. Name that additive.
exp: Water and spirit caramel are the only permitted additions after maturation, so a Scotch cannot be sweetened or flavoured the way some other categories legally can. The caramel exists to make batches look alike rather than to add taste, though whether it is genuinely tasteless is argued about at length.

q: Unmalted barley entered the Irish mash bill in the eighteenth century for a reason that had nothing to do with flavour. What drove it?
opts: A duty levied on malted grain
An excise ban on triple distillation
A shortage of peat for kilning
exp: The tax was charged on malt, so distillers cut the mash with raw barley and lowered the bill. What began as tax avoidance became the defining texture of Irish single pot still whiskey, which is creamy and spiced in a way an all-malt mash is not.

q: American regulations cap the strength at which bourbon may come off the still, and again the strength at which it may go into the barrel. Which pair of figures is correct?
opts: 140 proof off the still and 110 proof into the barrel
160 proof off the still and 125 proof into the barrel
125 proof off the still and 160 proof into the barrel
190 proof off the still and 160 proof into the barrel
exp: That is 80 percent alcohol off the still and 62.5 percent into the wood, with a bottling floor of 80 proof. Entry strength matters because a lower one pulls different compounds out of the oak, which is why some distillers barrel well under the ceiling.

q: The word straight on an American whiskey label carries an ageing requirement that plain bourbon does not have to meet. How long?
accept: two years in new charred oak
exp: Two years in new charred oak, with corn whiskey the single exception, and if a straight whiskey is younger than four years the label has to state its age. Bourbon itself has no ageing minimum at all, so a spirit is legally bourbon the moment it goes into the barrel.

q: One American designation demands a single distilling season at one distillery, four years in a federally supervised warehouse, and bottling at exactly 100 proof. Name it.
exp: The Bottled-in-Bond Act of 1897 was a consumer protection measure at a time when whiskey was routinely adulterated, and the government put its own supervision behind the label. It is why so many bonded bottlings sit at exactly fifty percent alcohol.

q: A bottle sold as American blended whiskey may be mostly neutral spirit, but a floor is set for the real whiskey in it. What is that floor?
exp: The remaining four fifths may be grain neutral spirit, which is why the category sits well below straight whiskey in both price and character. Canadian blends answer to a different rule and Scotch blends to another again, so the word blended means something different in each country.

q: An American spirit built on a mash of at least eighty percent corn may be sold with no wood ageing at all, and if it is aged the barrel must be used or uncharred. Name that category.
exp: The uncharred or used barrel is the whole point: new charred oak is what makes bourbon, so this category is deliberately kept away from it and stays close to its raw distillate. Most of it is sold white, and it is the legal descendant of American moonshine.

q: A tier was added to the Cognac ladder in 2018, sitting above XO and carrying a fourteen-year floor. What is it called?
exp: The same reform lifted XO itself from six years to ten, which left Napoleon standing on the six-year step XO had vacated. Hors d'Age is treated as equal to XO rather than as a step of its own, so it takes the same ten-year floor, and Fine Champagne describes the crus blended rather than any age at all.

q: Four grapes carry the Armagnac plantings, and one of them is a hybrid, the only such vine allowed in a French appellation spirit. Which?
exp: Baco Blanc, also called Baco 22A, crosses Folle Blanche with an American vine and was bred after phylloxera to work the sandy soils of Bas-Armagnac. It was due to be swept away by the EU ban on hybrid vines and was kept for Armagnac alone.
